issues.legal_issue: The statutory expression covering dealings with protected tribal immovable property includes possession that would extinguish a tribal owner's title and vest it in a non-tribal person.
material_facts: The land was originally held by members of a scheduled tribe in a tribal area.
The applicable protective regulation defined a transfer to include not only specified modes of transfer but also any other non-testamentary dealing with the property.
The defendant, a non-tribal person, occupied part of the land and claimed that his possession had extinguished the owner's title by adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: A dealing that deprives a tribal owner of title and vests it in a non-tribal person falls within the broad statutory meaning of transfer of immovable property; adverse possession may therefore constitute a prohibited transfer.
issues.legal_principle: Regulation 2(f) of the Orissa Scheduled Areas Transfer of Immovable Property (By Scheduled Tribes) Regulations, 1956, broadly defines transfer to include any dealing with the property. Regulation 3 prohibits a transfer of tribal immovable property to a non-tribal without prior written consent, and Regulation 3A provides for ejectment of unauthorized occupants. The Court applied an object-oriented construction to protective legislation, relying on Sanjay Dinkar Asarkar v. State of Maharashtra, Pandey Orson v. Ram Chander Sahu, Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka, Lingappa Pochanna Appelwar v. State of Maharashtra, Gamini Krishnayya v. Guraza Seshachalam, and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Babu Lal. It held that a broad construction gives effect to the protective purpose of the law.

predicates.civil_dispute_over_tribal_property: The dispute concerns rights in immovable property held by a member of a protected tribal community.
predicates.property_belonged_to_a_tribal_owner: The property was owned by a member of a tribal community protected by the applicable law.
predicates.nontribal_possession_would_extinguish_th: A non-tribal person's possession, if treated as adverse, would extinguish the tribal owner's title and vest it in that person.
predicates.deprivation_of_tribal_title_by_nontribal: Possession by a non-tribal person that deprives a tribal owner of title is treated as a prohibited dealing with the property.

issues.definition: When a civil dispute concerns protected tribal property and non-tribal possession would extinguish the tribal owner's title, that deprivation is treated as a prohibited property dealing.

issues.legal_issue: A non-tribal person cannot acquire title by adverse possession over property while it belongs to a tribal owner, and the period for a claim against a later non-tribal owner runs only after a valid transfer out of tribal ownership.
material_facts: The land belonged to tribal owners and then to a tribal successor before it was transferred with the required permission to a non-tribal purchaser.
The defendant was a non-tribal person and was assumed to have possessed the disputed property for more than twelve years by the time the suit was filed.
Only six years had elapsed between the authorized transfer to the non-tribal purchaser and the filing of the suit.
The High Court held that the defendant had perfected title by adverse possession, but the Supreme Court rejected that conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The defendant could not acquire title by adverse possession for the period during which the land belonged to tribal owners. The limitation period against the later non-tribal owner began after the authorized transfer, and the suit was not barred because only six years had elapsed by its institution.
issues.legal_principle: Article 65 and Section 27 of the Limitation Act, 1963, ordinarily govern acquisition of title by adverse possession and extinguishment of the owner's title. Regulation 7-D extended the period applicable to property belonging to a scheduled tribe, but did not authorize a non-tribal person to acquire title against a tribal owner. Regulations 3 and 3A prohibit the relevant deprivation of tribal property and provide for restoration; the protective provisions prevail over the general limitation rule to the extent of conflict. The Court also referred to Article 244 and paragraph 5 of the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution, Section 7 of the Orissa Merged States' Laws Act, 1950, Madhavrao Waman Saundalgekar v. Raghunath Venkatesh Deshpande, and Karimullakhan v. Bhanupratapsingh. It distinguished Laxmi Gouda v. Dandasi Goura and Madhia Nayak v. Arjuna Pradhan because those cases addressed the effect of the limitation amendment, not whether a non-tribal could acquire tribal property by adverse possession.

predicates.title_suit_based_on_ownership: The proceeding is a suit seeking possession of immovable property on the basis of title.
predicates.nontribal_claimant_possessed_property_wh: A non-tribal claimant possessed the property during a period when it belonged to a tribal owner.
predicates.property_was_later_validly_transferred_t: The property was subsequently transferred from a tribal owner to a non-tribal owner with the required permission.
predicates.ordinary_adverse_possession_period_had_n: The legally relevant period of adverse possession against the later non-tribal owner had not elapsed when the suit was brought.
predicates.nontribal_adverse_title_does_not_accrue_: A non-tribal claimant does not acquire adverse title during tribal ownership, and a suit filed before the applicable period runs after a valid transfer is not barred.

issues.definition: If a non-tribal claimant possessed property during tribal ownership, the property was later validly transferred to a non-tribal owner, and the relevant period had not elapsed after transfer, adverse title does not accrue during tribal ownership and the later title suit is not barred.

issues.legal_issue: When the extent of an encroachment and the appropriate remedy for unauthorized construction have not been determined, the case should be remitted for demarcation and a decision between restoration and compensation.
material_facts: The parties disputed the extent of the land encroached upon because their properties were adjoining.
There were competing survey materials, and the High Court had made no specific finding on the extent of the encroachment.
The parties disputed the extent and timing of construction on the encroached land.
The trial court had not determined whether demolition and restoration of possession or compensation in lieu would be the appropriate relief.
issues.conclusion: The case was remanded to the trial court to establish the encroached area, using an available reliable map or a commissioner-assisted survey, and to decide whether to order demolition and restoration of possession or compensation. Any compensation is to be assessed by reference to the date of the Supreme Court judgment, and payment is a condition for allowing the encroachment and construction to remain.
issues.legal_principle: The Court directed a remand in the interests of justice because material questions about the extent of encroachment, construction, and appropriate relief had not been resolved. It required demarcation of the property and a determination, after hearing the parties and taking additional evidence if necessary, whether possession should be restored or compensation should be awarded in lieu.

predicates.appeal_from_dismissal_of_title_suit: The proceeding is an appeal after a title suit was dismissed.
predicates.extent_of_encroachment_is_unresolved: The lower court has not determined the precise area of land encroached upon.
predicates.appropriate_relief_for_construction_is_u: The lower court has not determined whether unauthorized construction should be removed with possession restored or left in place on payment of compensation.
predicates.trial_court_must_determine_the_encroache: The case is remitted for the trial court to demarcate the encroachment and determine whether restoration or compensation is appropriate.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows dismissal of a title suit and the extent of encroachment and remedy for construction remain unresolved, the trial court must determine the encroached area and choose between restoration and compensation.
